top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B011) credits a new explanatory framework: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and turn small shocks into large, persistent fluctuations. It is close to thirty years old and has been reused widely as a building block, and the credit comes from one two-author paper, so no boundary has to be drawn through a diffuse literature. The main reservations are indirect identification, because the channel is established as a mechanism and not as a measured magnitude, and possible overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. Both can be handled by a citation limited to the collateral-price feedback that claims neither the accelerator strand nor an effect size. P002 (Helpman and Melitz, B005) is a close second. Its selection and reallocation margins have been tested more directly on firm-level data, but its attribution is harder to draw: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited, and Helpman's marginal credit must be separated from Krugman 2008 and from B020. P003 (B014) is the strongest labour candidate. It ranks third because the task-based and trade-shock strands may be two achievements under a three-name cap, the China-shock magnitudes are still debated, and Acemoglu and Restrepo are uncredited. P000 is last because at least two proposals are mature, serious and defensibly attributed.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; B014, ranked third, is adjacent to my field of labour economics, but this is field proximity and not a personal connection, and I list no co-authorship with any credited name on P001, P002 or P003
